newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche seen trailing rivals' 96 profits growth.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche seen trailing rivals' 96 profits growth.

text.p: The cost of last year's debacle at Deutsche Bank AG's London fund management unit MGAM is likely to have kept 1996 earnings at Germany's biggest bank trailing far behind its big domestic rivals.

Analysts expect Germany's largest bank to report a stagnation in 1996 net profit at the 1995 level of 2.1 billion marks ($1.28 billion) due in part to the 200 million-pound cost of compensating investors for allaged mismanagement at three MGAM unit trusts.
Its smaller rival Commerzbank AG is expected to post a net income gain of about 33 percent to 1.3 billion marks.
Commerzbank, Germany's third largest private sector bank, has said it will publish the management's dividend proposal and several key earnings figures for 1996 early on Tuesday.
Operating profit after risk provisions is expected to be up 47 percent to 2.12 billion marks, similar to nine-month earnings growth which was fuelled by gains in interest and commission income.
Most analysts expect the bank to recommend an unchanged 1.35 mark dividend and use the earnings gains to beef up reserves, possibly in preparation for buying an asset manager.
But some said Commerzbank might surprise the market with a small dividend hike even though chairman Martin Kohlhaussen said last year the bank planned an unchanged payout.
Dresdner Bank AG, Germany's second largest bank, will report key 1996 results on February 20 after a supervisory board meeting. Analysts see its 1996 net profit up about 30 percent.

Deutsche has in past years revealed its dividend proposal at the end of January but remained tight-lipped on Monday about whether it would release dividend or earnings figures after a supervisory board meeting on Tuesday.

The bank has already estimated that its subsidiary Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) will have to pay 200 million pounds in compensation to investors for alleged mismanagement of three European unit trusts by former MGAM fund manager Peter Young.
Deutsche plans to take the payment onto its 1996 accounts. The problem at MGAM, which came to light last September, was the latest in a string of blows to Deutsche's earnings in 1996.
The bank is estimated to have added more than 200 million marks to risk provisions to cover a bail-out of engineering group Kloeckner-Humboldt-Deutz AG (KHD).

Also, two major shareholdings, Daimler-Benz AG and construction group Philipp Holzmann AG, omitted dividends for 1995, costing Deutsche 219 million marks in lost income, according to analysts' estimates.
"It is clear that Deutsche's net profit will be unchanged, anything else would be very surprising," said Stefan Ermisch, banking analyst at WestLB in Duesseldorf.
"KHD, the ommission of the Daimler und Holzmann dividends, the MGAM affair, that must all be digested."

Dieter Hein, banking analyst at BHF-Bank, expects Deutsche to offset the cost of the MGAM debacle by realising gains on shareholdings last year. The bank has repeatedly said it wants to reduce its industrial shareholdings.

Despite the outlook for stagnant earnings and the recent upset caused by the departure of MGAM fund manager Nicola Horlick, Deutsche shares skyrocketed this year, up almost 19 percent from early January to 85.15 marks at Monday's close.

Ermisch has an "outperform" rating for Deutsche, arguing that its strategy of expanding its London-based investment banking arm Deutsche Morgan Grenfell is the right way to stay competitive in the global market.
Commerzbank's shares, rated market performer by Ermisch but outperform by Olaf Conrad at Morgan Stanley, have gained 13 percent this year. Dresdner has risen almost 18 percent.
Analysts and share traders say the gains are partly due to investors shifting funds from chemicals shares into banking stocks which were relative underperformers in 1996.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($1=1.6375 Mark)
